newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Peak output leads to bearish EU oil stocks in Jan.
newsitem.headline: Peak output leads to bearish EU oil stocks in Jan.

text.p: Peak refinery output this winter has resulted in comprehensively bearish European Union oil stock levels at the end of January, analysts and traders said on Tuesday.
"Without a cold end to the winter, it's looking pretty bearish," said Keith Hamm, managing director of oil consultants Petroleum Economics.

Crude and oil product stock levels rose 5.90 million barrels, or 0.6 percent, in January to 1,031.36 million barrels, Stichting Euroilstock said in its latest monthly report published on Tuesday. The rise left stocks 13.47 million barrels, or 1.3 percent, above year-ago levels.
Middle distillate stocks took a seasonal dip, but were still 7.94 million barrels, or 2.8 percent, above the levels in January 1996.

Traders and analysts say heating oil consumers and wholesalers bought extensively at the end of December and the start of January, but mostly resisted during the cold first half of the month and expressed almost no interest during the mild weather since.
"They're really rather bearish. It looks like the (near-capacity) refinery runs were maintained and the mild weather left heating oil stocks high," said Hamm.

Crude intake of 11.510 million barrels per day indicates a capacity utilisation rate of 91.35 percent in January, against 89.61 percent last year. Output has been high since early autumn when margins were healthy and low gas oil stocks on both sides of the Atlantic suggested healthy heating oil prices this winter.
Crude oil stocks, which rose by 3.43 million barrels, or 0.9 percent, in January, are also returning from a period of tightness, despite high refinery runs.
"We're back in the normal range," said Geoff Pyne, energy analyst at Swiss bank UBS.
The only hint of bullishness is gasoline, but even there the prospects are dim.
Stock levels were 5.61 million barrels, or 3.3 percent, below year-ago levels, but a build of 8.16 million barrels, or 5.2 percent, highlights the oversupply inherent in Europe.
"If you're a bull, you wouldn't give up hope, but it's very hard to be very positive about gasoline on this side of the Atlantic," said Pyne of UBS.
